Sbt 2 and boot-layout detectionRead closely

Works out which jar files make up the sbt launcher's "boot" classpath so the build can run fully offline. sbt 1 and sbt 2 lay these files out differently (sbt 1 uses unversioned names like scala-compiler.jar, sbt 2 uses versioned Scala 3 jar names), and there's no documented way to map them back to their Maven source — so the code asks the launcher for its real file list and matches files to resolved dependencies by content hash. Also covers the sbt 1 vs sbt 2 API differences needed to make the same manifest script run on both. This step lives inside the same `computeSbtLock` function and Nix build path as the next category, but it's the subtlest part of the PR, flagged in the code and docs as the part most likely to break on a future sbt release — read this part slowly.

Relevant files

  • cli/scala-cli-nix.scala
  • CONTRIBUTING.md

When sbt starts, the launcher jar first builds itself a boot directory: a folder of jars holding sbt's own Scala compiler and sbt's own code. Normally it downloads those jars. Inside the Nix sandbox there is no network, so we have to hand it a finished boot directory instead — the right files, at the right paths.

The hard part is that the launcher does not name those files the way Maven does, and sbt 1 and sbt 2 disagree about the naming. sbt 1's lib/ has plain scala-compiler.jar; sbt 2's has scala3-compiler_3-3.9.0.jar. There is no documented mapping back to the Maven artifact the bytes came from.

So this category stops guessing. At lock time the manifest task asks the running launcher for its real file list and the boot directory it lives in. The CLI then resolves the Maven side (org.scala-sbt:sbt, the Scala compiler, the compiler bridge), hashes everything, and matches each boot file to an artifact by content hash — the launcher renames files but never rewrites their bytes. The result is a list of (path, url, sha256) triples in the lockfile, which Nix replays as a symlink farm.

flowchart TD
  A["sbt manifest task<br/>(appConfiguration.provider)"] -->|"bootDirectory + relative file paths"| B["computeSbtLock"]
  C["Coursier: org.scala-sbt:sbt,<br/>scalaInstance, compilerBridge"] -->|"url + sha256 per artifact"| B
  B -->|"match on sha256"| D["bootFiles:<br/>(path, url, sha256)"]
  D --> E["lib.nix mkSbtBootDir:<br/>symlink farm at those paths"]

If a boot file matches nothing, the CLI fails loudly at lock time rather than shipping a gap — a missing boot file shows up in the sandbox as sbt#4955 or a NoClassDefFoundError, far from the cause.

Boot layout detection

Lockfile shape for the boot directory

SbtBootFile(path, url, sha256) is the whole trick in a data type: path is where the launcher wants the file (relative to the boot root), url is the Maven artifact supplying those bytes. SbtToolchainLock holds it alongside a deliberately separate bootCoursierCache:

  • bootFiles — only the files the launcher itself keeps. One evicted or duplicate-artifactId jar in that directory is enough to make sbt-launch die.
  • bootCoursierCache — the full transitive resolution (jars plus POMs, evicted versions included), which populates COURSIER_CACHE so sbt's own resolution works offline.

The same block adds the per-module and whole-lockfile types; those belong to the lock format rather than to boot detection, and the doc comments explain each field.

Which coordinates to resolve

Two small helpers pick Maven coordinates from a Scala version, dispatching on the major version and erroring on anything that isn't 2 or 3.

scalaInstanceDeps(scalaVersion): List[Dependency] — the compiler sbt will invoke. Scala 3 needs scala3-compiler_3 and scaladoc_3 (sbt puts both on the instance classpath); Scala 2 gets scala-compiler, which pulls the rest in transitively.

compilerBridgeDep(scalaVersion, sbtVersion): Dependency — note the asymmetry: Scala 3's bridge is versioned by compiler version, Scala 2's by sbt version (compiler-bridge_2.12 at the sbt version), because sbt compiles that one itself on first use.

3255+/** Coordinates whose resolution yields the Zinc `scalaInstance` for a given
3256+ * Scala version — the compiler sbt will invoke. For Scala 3 that is
3257+ * `scala3-compiler` plus `scaladoc` (sbt puts both on the instance's
3258+ * classpath); for Scala 2 the single `scala-compiler` artifact pulls in what
3259+ * it needs transitively.
3260+ */
3261+private def scalaInstanceDeps(scalaVersion: String): List[Dependency] =
3262+ scalaVersion.takeWhile(_ != '.') match {
3263+ case "3" =>
3264+ List(
3265+ Dependency.of("org.scala-lang", "scala3-compiler_3", scalaVersion),
3266+ Dependency.of("org.scala-lang", "scaladoc_3", scalaVersion)
3267+ )
3268+ case "2" =>
3269+ List(Dependency.of("org.scala-lang", "scala-compiler", scalaVersion))
3270+ case other =>
3271+ sys.error(s"scala-cli-nix: unsupported Scala major version '$other'")
3272+ }
3273+
3274+/** Compiler bridge coordinates. Scala 3 publishes a prebuilt bridge per
3275+ * compiler version; Scala 2's bridge is published per *sbt* version and is
3276+ * compiled by sbt on first use, which is why its sources have to be in the
3277+ * offline cache too.
3278+ */
3279+private def compilerBridgeDep(
3280+ scalaVersion: String,
3281+ sbtVersion: String
3282+): Dependency =
3283+ scalaVersion.takeWhile(_ != '.') match {
3284+ case "3" =>
3285+ Dependency.of("org.scala-lang", "scala3-sbt-bridge", scalaVersion)
3286+ case "2" =>
3287+ val binaryVersion = scalaVersion.split('.').take(2).mkString(".")
3288+ Dependency.of(
3289+ "org.scala-sbt",
3290+ s"compiler-bridge_$binaryVersion",
3291+ sbtVersion
3292+ )
3293+ case other =>
3294+ sys.error(s"scala-cli-nix: unsupported Scala major version '$other'")
3295+ }

Both are called over scalaVersions, which is the modules' Scala versions union sbt's own scalaBootVersion (cli/scala-cli-nix.scala:3317). That union is what makes sbt 2 work at all: sbt 2 runs on Scala 3.9.0, which no project module need use, yet its lib/ still needs that compiler stack.

Resolve, hash, match

This is the part to read slowly. Inside computeSbtLock, in order:

  1. Resolve org.scala-sbt:sbt-launch:<v> and find the launcher jar by filename; error if absent.
  2. Resolve org.scala-sbt:sbt:<v> — sbt's own boot closure.
  3. Resolve the scalaInstance and compiler bridge for every Scala version in play.
  4. Hash the launcher jar; run collectEntries over the boot artifacts to get the full cache set (jars + POMs).
  5. Build a sha256 -> url map from the boot cache, the scalaInstance and the bridge entries, then hash each boot file the manifest reported and look it up.

Two details worth checking: the map is keyed by hash, so if two artifacts ever had identical bytes under different URLs one would silently win — harmless here, since either URL fetches the same bytes. And the lookup miss is a hard sys.error with a long explanation, not a skip.

Documentation

CONTRIBUTING.md gains two sections, and they are the real payload of this category — the reasons behind the code above, written down so nobody re-derives them.

The first is sbt 1 vs sbt 2: nine concrete API differences that let one manifest script run on both, each with the misleading error it produces when you get it wrong. The short version: task keys must be vals and must carry @transient (sbt 2 caches task results to disk), bare statements are illegal in an sbt 2 .sbt file, --server is needed so you don't talk to an already-loaded build, reload plugins is gone, plugin artifact names are suffixed differently, packageBin / artifactPath is a virtual file ref rather than a File, and sbt's own Scala is a Scala 3. The code those notes describe lives in the manifest script and is explained in its own category.

The second is Hard-won pitfalls, which documents the boot-layout rule itself and the two earlier wrong turns: the boot directory must be named scala-<version> (the launcher recovers the version by substring), and lib/ filenames differ per sbt generation. Both failed as sbt#4955, which reads as a resolution failure and isn't one. The same pitfall list also covers the build side — pkgs.sbt being the wrong launcher, -Dsbt.offline=true, batch mode coming from JVM flags, sbt logging errors to stdout.

434+#### sbt 1 vs sbt 2
435+
436+Both are supported, and verified against sbt 1.10.7 (`examples/sbt`, `examples/sbt-multi`) and sbt 2.1.0 (the `smellar` project). sbt 2 differs in enough load-bearing ways to be worth listing, because most of them fail in misleading ways:
437+
438+- **Task keys must be `val`s.** `TaskKey[Unit]("scnManifest") := ...` compiles on sbt 2 and then isn't addressable — `Not a valid key: scnManifest`, as though the file were never read. sbt 2 builds its key index from the build definition's `val` declarations. `val scnManifest = taskKey[Unit](...)` works on both.
439+- **Bare statements are illegal** at the top level of an sbt 2 `.sbt` file; a stray `println(...)` is a compile error. Only declarations.
440+- **`@transient` on the key is mandatory.** sbt 2 caches task results to disk. Without the annotation the manifest task doesn't even compile — sbt 2 wants an `sjsonnew.HashWriter` for the whole input tuple, and there is none for `ResolvedProject` / `ModuleID` / `VirtualFileRef`. Worse, if one were found, the *second* lock of an unchanged project would be a cache hit: `[success] ... cache 100%, 1 disk cache hit`, no output at all, and we'd fail on the missing sentinels. sbt 2 suggests `@transient` or `Def.uncached`; only the former exists on sbt 1, which ignores it as a plain Scala annotation.
441+- **`--server` is required.** For sbt 2 the launcher defaults to the native thin client (`sbtn`), which talks to a persistent background server. A server started *before* we wrote `scn-manifest.sbt` serves its already-loaded build definition, so the task isn't there — the same misleading `Not a valid key`. `--server` forces the in-process JVM sbt, which also means we never attach to or disturb a developer's running sbt session. (This bites sbt 1 users too, any time Metals or BSP has a server up.)
442+- **`reload plugins` / `reload return` are gone.** sbt 2 rejects the command line outright ("Expected end of input"), so the meta-build can't be navigated that way. Plugins are instead read from the main build via `Project.extract(state).currentUnit.unit.plugins.pluginData.report`, which works on both and needs no second sbt startup.
443+- **Plugin artifact names differ.** sbt 1's update report names a plugin unsuffixed (`com.eed3si9n:sbt-buildinfo:0.13.1`) plus `sbtVersion` / `scalaVersion` marker attributes, and the published artifact is `sbt-buildinfo_2.12_1.0`. sbt 2 reports the suffixed name directly (`sbt-assembly_sbt2_3`) with no markers. Requiring *both* markers to be present is what distinguishes the two cases — and it also excludes artifacts that merely carry other extra attributes, like `scala3-sbt-bridge` with its `info.*` ones.
444+- **`packageBin / artifactPath` is an `xsbti.VirtualFileRef`** on sbt 2, not a `File`, and its `toString` is placeholder-based (`${OUT}/jvm/scala-3.9.0/...`). `fileConverter` exists on both and maps either to a real path, so nothing has to know what `${OUT}` expands to. Everything else we read — `baseDirectory`, `unmanagedSources`, `unmanagedResourceDirectories` — is still a `File` on both.
445+- **sbt 2's output tree is `target/out/<platform>/scala-<v>/<project>/`**, not `target/scala-<v>/`. Nothing in the build side cares, because the jar path comes from sbt rather than from a glob — which is precisely why it comes from sbt.
446+- **sbt's own Scala is a Scala 3** on sbt 2 (`scalaBootVersion` = 3.9.0 for sbt 2.1.0, versus 2.12.x for sbt 1). That is why `scalaBootVersion` joins the modules' Scala versions when resolving `scalaInstance` and the compiler bridge: sbt's `lib/` needs its own compiler stack, whose version need not match anything the project compiles with.
447+
448+#### Hard-won pitfalls
449+
450+These cost real time and are worth not rediscovering:
451+
452+- **Don't derive the boot layout from Maven coordinates — ask the launcher.** `lock-sbt` records sbt's boot directory as a list of `(path, url, sha256)` taken from `appConfiguration.value.provider` (`scalaProvider.jars` for `lib/`, `mainClasspath` for the app jars), and recovers each file's origin by matching its *content hash* against the resolved artifacts. The launcher renames files on the way in, so names prove nothing — sbt 1's `lib/scala-library.jar` is Maven's `scala-library-2.12.20.jar`, sbt 2's is `scala-library-3.9.0.jar` — but the bytes are untouched. Reconstructing the layout by hand was wrong twice before this (see the two entries below), and each time the symptom was sbt#4955, which reads as a resolution failure and isn't one.
453+- **The boot directory name is load-bearing** — the first way the above went wrong. It must be `scala-<scalaBootVersion>`, not `<scalaBootVersion>`. The launcher accepts *any* directory under the boot root, then recovers the Scala version by taking the substring after the last `"scala-"` in that directory's name (`BootConfiguration.extractScalaVersion`, with `ScalaVersionPrefix = "scala-"`). A bare `2.12.20` is accepted and then yields no version, reported as **sbt#4955**: "sbt launcher is unable to detect the Scala version for org.scala-sbt:sbt; this likely indicates an incomplete artifact resolution and/or corrupt boot cache". Resolution was complete and the cache was fine.
454+- **`lib/` filenames differ per sbt generation** — the second way. sbt 1 wants *unversioned* `scala-compiler.jar`, `scala-library.jar` and `scala-reflect.jar` plus a versioned `scala-xml_2.12-<v>.jar`; sbt 2 wants versioned Scala 3 names (`scala3-compiler_3-<v>.jar`, `scala3-library_3-<v>.jar`, `scala3-interfaces-<v>.jar`, `tasty-core_3-<v>.jar`, `scala-asm-<v>.jar`) plus an unversioned `scala-library.jar`. Hence: ask the launcher.
455+- **sbt#4955 for the reason it actually documents.** It also fires when the boot directory contains *any* evicted-version or duplicate-artifactId jar. That's why `bootFiles` holds only what the launcher itself keeps, while `bootCoursierCache` carries the full transitive set (with POMs and evicted versions) for sbt's own resolution.
456+- **`pkgs.sbt` is the wrong launcher for the sandbox.** It's bundled with one specific Scala bootstrap version and will try to fetch a different one over the network whenever `project/build.properties` points elsewhere. We lock and exec the matching `sbt-launch-<sbtVersion>.jar` directly. `pkgs.sbt` is fine at *lock* time, where there's a network.
457+- **`-Dsbt.offline=true` matters.** Without it lm-coursier still reaches for the network at update time and chokes on the HTML error page with the baffling `SAXParseException: DOCTYPE is disallowed`. The real error underneath is `UnknownHostException`.
458+- **`sbt update` resolves all configurations at once.** It's per-project, but asking for `app/package` still resolves `app`'s Test configuration. So the *build* cache needs each closure module's test dependencies too, even though nothing there compiles tests (`sbtModuleAllDeps`). The runtime *classpath*, by contrast, takes only the main scope — munit has no business on an app's classpath.
459+- **`mkCacheDir` with an empty list produces no `$out`.** It emits one `mkdir`+`ln` per artifact, so an empty dependency list yields an empty builder and the derivation fails. Projects without plugins get no plugin cache layered in at all, rather than an empty one.
460+- **Batch mode and colors come from JVM flags, not CLI flags.** `-no-colors` / `-batch` are understood by the `sbt` shell script, not by `sbt-launch.jar`. The equivalents are `-Dsbt.color=false`, `-Dsbt.supershell=false`, and closing stdin (`< /dev/null`).
461+- **sbt logs errors to stdout.** `lock-sbt` captures stdout (that's where the manifest comes from) and only forwards stderr, so a failure replays the captured stdout into the exception. Without that, a broken build definition shows up as a bare "sbt exited with code 1".

The notes match the code: the prose claims about bootFiles vs bootCoursierCache, the hash matching, and the scala-<version> directory name all line up with the snippets above and with mkSbtBootDir in lib.nix:543, which carries the same warning as a comment.

Sbt lock and buildRead through

The new `lock-sbt` CLI command runs sbt once (via a small generated script) to read every module's sources, dependencies, and plugins, and writes that into a lockfile; the matching `buildSbtApp`/`buildSbtApps` Nix functions then build the project offline from that lockfile. This orchestration sits in the same function (`computeSbtLock`) and the same Nix build path as the boot-layout matching above — that step is covered there in closer detail, so treat this as one continuous read rather than two separate passes. Includes two new example projects (a single-module and a three-module sbt build) that exercise the round trip, plus the doc updates explaining the new path. Real new logic, but it closely follows the existing lock/build pattern already used for plain scala-cli projects.

What this category does

Two halves of one round trip for sbt projects. At lock time (network available) scn lock-sbt writes a throwaway scn-manifest.sbt into the project, runs sbt once, and reads back a JSON description of the whole build — every module's sources, resource dirs, Scala version, main class, jar path, dependsOn edges, library deps, plus the plugin closure and sbt's own boot file list. The CLI then resolves and hashes all of that through the same Coursier pipeline the scala-cli path already uses, and writes a kind = "sbt" lockfile.

At build time buildSbtApp reads that lockfile, materializes an offline sbt installation from it, and runs real sbt inside the sandbox (java -jar sbt-launch.jar with one <id>/package target per module in the build closure) — we don't try to reimplement an sbt build definition. The jars sbt produces get copied out and wrapped as $out/bin/<pname>.

flowchart TD
  sbt["real sbt, lock time (network)"] -->|"scn-manifest.sbt task → sentinel JSON"| cli["computeSbtLock"]
  cli -->|"Coursier resolve + sha256"| lock["scala.lock.json, kind = sbt"]
  lock -->|loadSbtLock + fetchurl| tc["mkSbtToolchain:<br/>boot dir + coursier cache"]
  lock -->|"sources, modules, plugins"| bld["buildSbtAppImpl"]
  tc --> bld
  bld -->|"java -jar sbt-launch, one &lt;id&gt;/package per closure module"| out["$out/bin/&lt;pname&gt; + share/*.jar"]

The one piece not explained here is how boot files are matched back to artifacts by content hash — that is the bootFiles / sbt-2 work covered in Sbt 2 and boot-layout detection, including the new lockfile case classes (SbtLockFile, SbtToolchainLock, SbtModuleLock, SbtBootFile) that both halves read and write.

Lock side (CLI)

lock-sbt takes the same repository flags as lock plus -o, and nothing else — no --platform or --scala-version, since an sbt build picks those itself.

The heart of the lock phase is the injected sbt task plus its runner. runSbtManifest(projectDir): IO[SbtManifest] writes scn-manifest.sbt, runs sbt --server -no-colors -batch scnManifest, deletes the file in a guarantee, pulls the payload from between two sentinel lines, and decodes it. The task itself uses ScopeFilter(inAnyProject) + .all(...) so one invocation reports every project in the build, and prints hand-rolled JSON (no JSON library is available in a .sbt file without resolving one).

Several details are load-bearing and worth reading rather than summarizing: @transient val scnManifest (sbt 2 builds its key index from vals and caches task results to disk), --server (sbt 2's default thin client would reuse a server that loaded the build before we wrote the file), Compile / unmanagedSources instead of sources (the latter includes generated files under target/, which don't exist in the sandbox), the realPath helper bridging sbt 1's java.io.File and sbt 2's VirtualFileRef, and the plugin-name reconstruction that differs between sbt generations. This block also contains transitiveInternalDeps (tail-recursive closure of dependsOn, cycle-safe, sorted) and sbtCommand, which reads SCALA_CLI_NIX_SBT.

2911+//

2923+/** The sbt task we inject to read the build, written to `scn-manifest.sbt` in
2924+ * the project root and deleted afterwards.
2925+ *
2926+ * `ScopeFilter(inAnyProject)` plus `.all(...)` is what makes this
2927+ * multi-module: every setting is read once per project in the build, in a
2928+ * stable order, so one task invocation describes the whole build. Note that
2929+ * sbt synthesizes an aggregate root project for the build's base directory
2930+ * when `build.sbt` doesn't define one; it shows up here like any other
2931+ * module, with no sources and no main class.
2932+ *
2933+ * Plugins are read from the same task, out of the loaded build's plugin data,
2934+ * rather than by running a second task inside the meta-build. `reload
2935+ * plugins` / `reload return` would be the idiomatic way to reach `project/`,
2936+ * but sbt 2 removed those commands.
2937+ *
2938+ * `Compile / unmanagedSources` (not `sources`) is deliberate: `sources`
2939+ * includes generated files under `target/`, which don't exist in the sandbox
2940+ * and would be recorded as phantom paths. Generators that are self-contained
2941+ * re-run inside the sandbox anyway.
2942+ *
2943+ * `Compile / packageBin / artifactPath` is a *setting*, so reading it costs
2944+ * nothing. `Compile / mainClass` is a task that compiles the project — which
2945+ * is why locking an sbt project builds it once, at lock time, where there is
2946+ * still a network.
2947+ *
2948+ * The key must be a `val` (`val scnManifest = taskKey[...]`) rather than
2949+ * constructed inline as `TaskKey[Unit]("scnManifest") := ...`. sbt 1 accepts
2950+ * either, but sbt 2 builds its key index from the build definition's `val`
2951+ * declarations, so the inline form compiles fine and then isn't addressable
2952+ * from the command line: `Not a valid key: scnManifest`.
2953+ *
2954+ * Statements have to be declarations too — a bare `println(...)` at the top
2955+ * level of a `.sbt` file is a compile error in sbt 2.
2956+ *

2962+ * that prints nothing, failing on the missing sentinels. `@transient` is the
2963+ * opt-out sbt 2 itself suggests (alongside `Def.uncached`, which sbt 1
2964+ * doesn't have); being a plain Scala annotation, sbt 1 just ignores it.
2965+ *
2966+ * JSON is printed by hand rather than via a library: the meta-build has no

2968+ * moment. Output is sentinel-delimited so sbt's own logging can be discarded.
2969+ *

3147+/** Transitive closure of the sbt projects `id` depends on, excluding `id`
3148+ * itself. `direct` maps each project id to its immediate `dependsOn` ids.
3149+ *
3150+ * Cycles can't occur in a well-formed sbt build, but a malformed one
3151+ * shouldn't hang the locker, so visited ids are tracked. The result is sorted
3152+ * for lockfile determinism; sbt works out the actual build order itself.
3153+ */
3154+def transitiveInternalDeps(
3155+ direct: Map[String, List[String]],
3156+ id: String
3157+): List[String] = {
3158+ @scala.annotation.tailrec
3159+ def loop(frontier: List[String], seen: Set[String]): Set[String] =
3160+ frontier match {
3161+ case Nil => seen
3162+ case next :: rest if seen.contains(next) => loop(rest, seen)
3163+ case next :: rest =>
3164+ loop(direct.getOrElse(next, Nil) ++ rest, seen + next)
3165+ }
3166+ (loop(direct.getOrElse(id, Nil), Set.empty) - id).toList.sorted
3167+}

3170+ * by the Nix wrapper; the PATH fallback keeps the CLI usable outside Nix.
3171+ *
3172+ * This is only ever the *lock-time* sbt, which has network access and simply
3173+ * bootstraps whatever `project/build.properties` asks for. The sbt that runs
3174+ * inside the sandbox is the locked `sbt-launch.jar` instead — see
3175+ * `SbtToolchainLock`.
3176+ */
3177+private def sbtCommand: String =
3178+ sys.env.getOrElse("SCALA_CLI_NIX_SBT", "sbt")
3179+
3180+private def extractSentinel(
3181+ out: String,
3182+ begin: String,
3183+ end: String,
3184+ what: String
3185+): IO[String] = {
3186+ val beginIdx = out.indexOf(begin)
3187+ val endIdx = out.indexOf(end)
3188+ if (beginIdx < 0 || endIdx < 0)
3189+ IO.raiseError(
3190+ new RuntimeException(
3191+ s"sbt output did not contain the $what sentinels. Output:\n$out"
3192+ )
3193+ )
3194+ else IO.pure(out.substring(beginIdx + begin.length, endIdx).trim)
3195+}

3197+/** Run the manifest task, returning the parsed build description.
3198+ *
3199+ * One sbt startup and one injected file. Reading the plugins from the main
3200+ * build (see `SbtManifestSbt`) is what keeps it to one: the obvious route,
3201+ * `reload plugins` / `reload return` around a task defined in `project/`,
3202+ * only works on sbt 1 — sbt 2 removed those commands and rejects the command
3203+ * line with "Expected end of input".
3204+ */
3205+private def runSbtManifest(projectDir: Path): IO[SbtManifest] = {
3206+ val manifestSbt = projectDir / "scn-manifest.sbt"
3207+ val runSbt =
3208+ ProcessBuilder(
3209+ sbtCommand,
3210+ // `--server` forces the in-process JVM sbt instead of the native thin
3211+ // client. For sbt 2 the launcher defaults to the client, which talks to
3212+ // a persistent background server — and a server started before we wrote
3213+ // `scn-manifest.sbt` serves its already-loaded build definition, so the
3214+ // task simply isn't there: `Not a valid key: scnManifest`. It also means
3215+ // we never attach to (or disturb) a developer's running sbt session.
3216+ List("--server", "-no-colors", "-batch", "scnManifest")
3217+ )
3218+ .withWorkingDirectory(projectDir)
3219+ .spawn[IO]
3220+ .use { proc =>
3221+ val stdout = proc.stdout.through(fs2.text.utf8.decode).compile.string
3222+ val stderr = proc.stderr.through(fs2.io.stderr[IO]).compile.drain
3223+ (stdout, stderr).parTupled.flatMap { (out, _) =>
3224+ proc.exitValue.flatMap { code =>
3225+ // sbt reports task and build-definition errors on *stdout*, which
3226+ // we capture rather than forward. Replaying it into the failure
3227+ // means a broken build definition says so instead of just
3228+ // surfacing an exit code.
3229+ IO.raiseError(
3230+ new RuntimeException(s"sbt exited with code $code. Output:\n$out")
3231+ ).whenA(code != 0)
3232+ .as(out)
3233+ }
3234+ }
3235+ }
3236+ (writeFile(manifestSbt, SbtManifestSbt) *> runSbt)
3237+ .guarantee(Files[IO].deleteIfExists(manifestSbt).void)
3238+ .flatMap { out =>
3239+ extractSentinel(out, SbtManifestBegin, SbtManifestEnd, "manifest")
3240+ .flatMap { payload =>
3241+ IO.fromEither(
3242+ parseJson(payload)
3243+ .flatMap(_.as[SbtManifest])
3244+ .leftMap(e =>
3245+ new RuntimeException(
3246+ s"Failed to parse the sbt manifest: $e\n$payload"
3247+ )

computeSbtLock(manifest): IO[String] turns the manifest into lockfile text:

  1. Log what sbt reported, per module.
  2. Per module, resolve twice — main scope, and main ∪ test — because the test cache needs both, and two modules can land on different winners for the same library.
  3. Resolve plugins with versions forced to what sbt already resolved, so Coursier can't evict a version sbt will ask for offline.
  4. Resolve the launcher jar, sbt's boot closure, the scalaInstances and compiler bridges (per distinct Scala version plus sbt's own), then match boot files by hash — see Sbt 2 and boot-layout detection.

prepareSbtSources sources resourceDirs src filters the source tree down to: root-level *.sbt, all of project/, the locked source files, and resource dirs — dropping every target/. The directory branch has to also let through ancestors of locked sources and resource dirs, or cleanSourceWith would prune a parent before reaching its children; that interplay is the part to check.

481+ # --- sbt support -----------------------------------------------------------
482+ #
483+ # Unlike the scala-cli path (where we drive the compiler ourselves), sbt
484+ # projects are built by running *real sbt* inside the sandbox: reimplementing
485+ # an sbt build definition is not tractable. That means the sandbox needs a
486+ # complete, offline sbt installation. `scn lock-sbt` records it; the helpers
487+ # below materialize it.
488+
489+ # Filter `src` down to what sbt needs to load the build and compile the
490+ # listed sources: every root-level `*.sbt`, the whole `project/` tree (the
491+ # meta-build, where plugins live), the locked source files, and any resource
492+ # directories. Build output dirs (`target/`) are dropped — they are the
493+ # sandbox's to create, and including a stale local one would both poison the
494+ # derivation hash and let sbt mistake prebuilt classes for fresh ones.
495+ prepareSbtSources = sources: resourceDirs: src:
496+ let
497+ isTargetPath = rel:
498+ rel == "target" || lib.hasSuffix "/target" rel || lib.hasInfix "/target/" rel;
499+ insideResourceDir = rel:
500+ builtins.any (r: rel == r || lib.hasPrefix (r + "/") rel) resourceDirs;
501+ ancestorOfResourceDir = rel:
502+ builtins.any (r: lib.hasPrefix (rel + "/") r) resourceDirs;
503+ ancestorOfSource = rel:
504+ builtins.any (s: lib.hasPrefix (rel + "/") s) sources;
505+ # sbt reads `*.sbt` from the build root and from `project/`, nowhere
506+ # else — a stray `foo/bar.sbt` inside a module is not part of the build
507+ # definition, so it has no reason to enter the source tree.
508+ isRootSbtFile = rel:
509+ lib.hasSuffix ".sbt" rel && !(lib.hasInfix "/" rel);
510+ in lib.cleanSourceWith {
511+ inherit src;
512+ filter = path: type:
513+ let rel = lib.removePrefix (toString src + "/") (toString path);
514+ in if isTargetPath rel then false
515+ else if type == "directory"
516+ then rel == "project"
517+ || lib.hasPrefix "project/" rel
518+ || ancestorOfSource rel
519+ || insideResourceDir rel
520+ || ancestorOfResourceDir rel
521+ else isRootSbtFile rel
522+ || lib.hasPrefix "project/" rel
523+ || builtins.elem rel sources
524+ || insideResourceDir rel;
525+ };

527+ # Reproduce sbt's boot directory exactly as the launcher laid it out. Each
528+ # entry carries the path the launcher wants (`scala-<v>/lib/scala-library.jar`,
529+ # `scala-<v>/org.scala-sbt/sbt/<ver>/main_3-<ver>.jar`, ...) and the artifact
530+ # supplying those bytes; `scn lock-sbt` recorded the pairing by content hash.
531+ #
532+ # Nothing here derives a filename from a coordinate, and deliberately so. The
533+ # launcher renames files on the way in, and the two sbt generations disagree
534+ # about how — sbt 1's `lib/` has unversioned scala-compiler/library/reflect,
535+ # sbt 2's has versioned Scala 3 names plus an unversioned scala-library.jar.
536+ # Guessing it wrong is not a clean failure either: the launcher reports
537+ # sbt#4955 ("unable to detect the Scala version for org.scala-sbt:sbt"),
538+ # which reads as a resolution problem and isn't one.
539+ #
540+ # Only resolved winners are in `bootFiles`, because that is all the launcher
541+ # itself keeps — an evicted or duplicate-artifactId jar in the boot directory
542+ # is what genuinely does provoke sbt#4955.
543+ mkSbtBootDir = name: bootFiles:
544+ let
545+ # `entry.dep.path` is the boot-relative path from the lockfile;
546+ # `entry.path` is the fetched store path. (`fetchAll` keeps the lockfile
547+ # object under `dep`, which is why both are called "path".)
548+ linkCommands = builtins.map (entry: ''
549+ mkdir -p $out/$(dirname "${entry.dep.path}")
550+ ln -sf ${entry.path} $out/${entry.dep.path}
551+ '') bootFiles;
552+ in runCommand name {} (builtins.concatStringsSep "\n" linkCommands);
553+ # Project-independent sbt environment: launcher jar + boot dir + a Coursier
554+ # cache prepopulated with everything sbt needs to bootstrap itself (the boot
555+ # transitive set including evicted POMs, the scalaInstance, and the compiler
556+ # bridge). The project's own dependencies and plugins are layered on top at
557+ # build time rather than merged in here, so that two projects sharing an sbt
558+ # version + Scala version + locked artifact set share these exact store
559+ # paths. The cache key deliberately excludes everything project-specific.
560+ mkSbtToolchain = sbtBlock:
561+ let
562+ key = "${sbtBlock.sbtVersion}-${sbtBlock.scalaBootVersion}";
563+ in {
564+ launcherJar = sbtBlock.launcherJar.path;
565+ inherit (sbtBlock) sbtVersion scalaBootVersion;
566+ bootDir = mkSbtBootDir "sbt-boot-${key}" sbtBlock.bootFiles;
567+ coursierCache = mkCacheDir "sbt-coursier-${key}"
568+ (sbtBlock.bootCoursierCache ++ sbtBlock.scalaInstance ++ sbtBlock.compilerBridge);
569+ };

Then the build itself. buildSbtAppImpl { pname, version, src, sources, resourceDirs, loaded, module, attrOverrides } returns a derivation that:

  1. computes the build closure (module + its transitive internalDependencies);
  2. layers caches on COURSIER_CACHE — the closure's all-configuration deps (sbt's update resolves Test even for package) plus the plugin cache;
  3. configure phase: mkSbtEnvSetup makes writable cp -rs copies of boot dir and cache, redirects HOME;
  4. build phase: a single java -jar sbt-launch.jar ... < /dev/null, whose arguments are packageTargets — one <id>/package per module in the build closure, not just the target module. sbt works out the build order itself;
  5. install phase: copy each closure module's packageBin to $out/share/<pname>/<id>.jar and makeWrapper a java -cp ... launcher — classpath takes only main-scope jars, deduped, POMs filtered out.

buildSbtTest is the same shape but runs a single <id>/test from a writable copy of the tree (sbt writes into target/, and cwd-relative test resources then resolve as usual), adding only that module's own test sources. It's attached via mkSbtTests as passthru.tests.test. The throws on a missing module, empty packageBin, or absent main class are where a stale lockfile surfaces.

The two public entry points are thin: buildSbtApp resolves module (defaulting only when the lockfile has exactly one) and delegates; buildSbtApps maps over modules that have a main class — skipping library modules and sbt's synthesized aggregate root, since a throwing attribute would break nix flake check for the whole flake.

943+ # Build one sbt module as an app, by running real sbt inside the Nix sandbox.
944+ # Requires a `kind = "sbt"` lockfile produced by `scn lock-sbt`.
945+ #
946+ # `module` names an sbt project id. It may be omitted only when the lockfile
947+ # has exactly one module — note that sbt synthesizes an aggregate root
948+ # project for builds whose `build.sbt` doesn't define one, so a two-module
949+ # build usually locks as three modules and needs `module` passed explicitly.
950+ #
951+ # The module's test scope, if it has one, is exposed as `passthru.tests.test`
952+ # and so is picked up by `collectChecks`.
953+ buildSbtApp = { pname, version, src, lockFile, module ? null, attrOverrides ? (attrs: _platform: attrs) }:
954+ let
955+ loaded = loadSbtLock lockFile;
956+ moduleNames = builtins.attrNames loaded.modules;
957+ resolvedModule =
958+ if module != null
959+ then module
960+ else if builtins.length moduleNames == 1
961+ then builtins.head moduleNames
962+ else builtins.throw "scala-cli-nix: lockfile has multiple sbt modules (${builtins.concatStringsSep ", " moduleNames}). Pass `module` to buildSbtApp or use buildSbtApps.";
963+ in buildSbtAppImpl {
964+ inherit pname version src loaded attrOverrides;
965+ module = resolvedModule;
966+ sources = loaded.sources;
967+ resourceDirs = loaded.resourceDirs;
968+ };
969+
970+ # Build every runnable sbt module from a lockfile, returning an attrset keyed
971+ # by sbt project id (dots normalized to underscores).
972+ #
973+ # Only modules with a main class are included: a library module and sbt's
974+ # synthesized aggregate root have nothing to run, and emitting entries that
975+ # throw on evaluation would break `nix flake check` for the whole flake.
976+ # Build a library module deliberately — if you need its jar on its own — by
977+ # naming it via `buildSbtApp`'s `module`.
978+ buildSbtApps = { pname, version, src, lockFile, attrOverrides ? (attrs: _platform: attrs) }:
979+ let
980+ loaded = loadSbtLock lockFile;
981+ runnable = builtins.filter
982+ (m: loaded.modules.${m}.mainClass != null)
983+ (builtins.attrNames loaded.modules);
984+ in builtins.listToAttrs (
985+ builtins.map (m:
986+ { name = nixKey m;
987+ value = buildSbtAppImpl {
988+ inherit pname version src loaded attrOverrides;
989+ module = m;
990+ sources = loaded.sources;
991+ resourceDirs = loaded.resourceDirs;
992+ };
993+ }
994+ ) runnable
995+ );

Tests

Two layers. A plain example-based munit suite covers transitiveInternalDeps in isolation: empty closure, direct dep, transitive chain, diamond (each module once), self-reference, a cycle (terminates instead of hanging), and an unknown id from a hand-edited lockfile.

CONTRIBUTING.md — head 7-8; head 341-433; head 464-470; base 345-345, head 477-477; base 347-347, head 479-479; head 509-510; base 436-437; head 571-582 (120 lines)
7+Three lockfile shapes share that split, discriminated by a top-level `kind`: `"scala-cli"` (the default, project sources driven by scala-cli), `"coursier-app"` (an app packaged straight from Coursier coordinates), and `"sbt"` (an sbt-managed project, built by running real sbt inside the sandbox).
8+
⋯ 332 lines
341+### `scala-cli-nix lock-sbt` (sbt path)
342+
343+A third lockfile shape, `kind = "sbt"`, for projects built by sbt rather than scala-cli. The split from the other two paths is fundamental: we don't drive the compiler ourselves, we run **real sbt inside the Nix sandbox**. Reimplementing an sbt build definition isn't tractable, so instead the lock phase captures a complete, offline sbt installation and the build phase hands it to the project's own sbt version.
344+
345+#### Lock phase
346+
347+`scn lock-sbt` shells out to sbt (from `SCALA_CLI_NIX_SBT`, set by the Nix wrapper to `pkgs.sbt`; falls back to `sbt` on PATH). It writes one throwaway task file, runs it, and deletes it again:
348+
349+- `scn-manifest.sbt` in the project root — the `scnManifest` task, invoked as `sbt --server -no-colors -batch scnManifest`. `ScopeFilter(inAnyProject)` plus `.all(...)` reads every setting once per project in the build, so a single invocation describes all modules. The key is a `@transient val` and the invocation forces `--server`; both are load-bearing on sbt 2 and explained under "sbt 1 vs sbt 2" below.
350+
351+The task prints hand-rolled JSON between sentinel lines (`##SCN_MANIFEST_BEGIN##` / `##SCN_MANIFEST_END##`) so sbt's own logging can be discarded. Hand-rolled because pulling in a JSON library would mean resolving it at an awkward moment.
352+
353+Notable details of what the manifest reports:
354+
355+- `Compile / unmanagedSources`, not `sources`. The latter includes generated files under `target/`, which don't exist in the sandbox and would be recorded as phantom paths. Self-contained source generators re-run inside the sandbox anyway — that's how the `sbt-multi` example's `BuildInfoPlugin` works.
356+- `Compile / packageBin / artifactPath`, relative to the build root. It's a *setting*, so reading it is free, and it names each module's jar exactly — which is what makes multi-module work, since several jars can be collected without ambiguity.
357+- `Compile / mainClass` is a *task* that compiles the project. Locking an sbt project therefore builds it once, at lock time, where there's still a network.
358+- Each project's `dependencies` (its `dependsOn` ids). The CLI turns these into a transitive closure per module (`transitiveInternalDeps`).
359+- `libraryDependencies` split by configuration: `% Test` (configurations starting with `test`) goes to the module's test scope, everything else — `None`, compile, runtime, default, provided, optional — to its main scope. Provided/optional deps land on the runtime classpath as a result; for a standalone app there's no container to supply them.
360+- Paths outside the build root are dropped: they have no in-sandbox equivalent.
361+
362+sbt synthesizes an aggregate root project for builds whose `build.sbt` doesn't define one. It appears in the lockfile like any other module, with no sources and no main class.
363+
364+The CLI then resolves, per module, the main scope and (main ∪ test) scope separately — two modules can legitimately land on different winners for the same library, and each needs its own winner in cache. On top of that it resolves the sbt-side artifacts described under "Toolchain" below.
365+
366+**Plugins.** Read from the same task, out of the loaded build's plugin data (`Project.extract(state).currentUnit.unit.plugins.pluginData.report`), rather than by running a task inside the meta-build — `reload plugins` would be the idiomatic route but sbt 2 removed it. `allModules` is already sbt's resolved meta-build closure, so the CLI pins every (group, artifact) to the version reported there and reproduces that resolution in one Coursier pass; letting Coursier reconcile freely could evict a version sbt still wants. Artifact naming differs between sbt generations — see "sbt 1 vs sbt 2". The meta-build's *non*-plugin dependencies (its own Scala compiler, compiler bridge, scala-xml, jline) need no separate locking: they all fall out of the `org.scala-sbt:sbt:<version>` resolution already captured in `bootCoursierCache`.
367+
368+#### Lockfile format (`kind = "sbt"`)
369+
370+```json
371+{
372+ "version": 9,
373+ "kind": "sbt",
374+ "sources": ["app/src/main/scala/app/Main.scala", "core/src/main/scala/core/Greeting.scala"],
375+ "resourceDirs": ["core/src/main/resources"],
376+ "modules": {
377+ "app": {
378+ "scalaVersion": "3.3.4",
379+ "mainClass": "app.Main",
380+ "packageBin": "app/target/scala-3.3.4/example-sbt-multi-app_3-0.1.0.jar",
381+ "internalDependencies": ["core"],
382+ "libraryDependencies": [ { "url": "...", "sha256": "..." } ],
383+ "test": {
384+ "sources": ["app/src/test/scala/app/MainTest.scala"],
385+ "resourceDirs": [],
386+ "libraryDependencies": [ { "url": "...", "sha256": "..." } ]
387+ }
388+ }
389+ },
390+ "pluginDependencies": [ { "url": "...", "sha256": "..." } ],
391+ "sbt": {
392+ "sbtVersion": "1.10.7",
393+ "scalaBootVersion": "2.12.20",
394+ "launcherJar": { "url": "...", "sha256": "..." },
395+ "bootFiles": [ { "path": "scala-3.9.0/lib/scala-library.jar", "url": "...", "sha256": "..." } ],
396+ "bootCoursierCache": [],
397+ "scalaInstance": [],
398+ "compilerBridge": []
399+ }
400+}
401+```
402+
403+There is no `targets` map: an sbt build picks its own platform and Scala version from `build.sbt`, so there's nothing to cross-build over. `modules` takes its place, keyed by sbt project id — even a single-project build gets exactly one entry.
404+
405+Field notes:
406+
407+- `sources` / `resourceDirs` are the **union** across modules' main scopes, because sbt loads and may compile the whole build even when asked for one module. Test sources stay per-module under `modules.<id>.test`.
408+- `internalDependencies` is the *transitive* closure of `dependsOn`, excluding the module itself, sorted for determinism (sbt works out the real build order).
409+- `pluginDependencies` is project-specific, so it sits at the top level rather than in `sbt`, where it would break toolchain sharing.
410+- No `exportHash`: there's no `scala-cli export --json` to hash. Staleness detection on this path is just "re-run `scn lock-sbt` and diff".
411+
412+#### Toolchain (`mkSbtToolchain`)
413+
414+Two read-only derivations keyed **only** on `(sbtVersion, scalaBootVersion)` plus the locked sbt-side artifact hashes — nothing project-specific. Two projects on the same sbt + Scala versions share these exact store paths, and changing user source code doesn't invalidate them.
415+
416+- `sbt-boot-<sbtVersion>-<scalaBootVersion>`: a symlink farm reproducing the launcher's boot layout verbatim, from the `(path, url, sha256)` triples in `bootFiles`. No filename is derived from a coordinate here — see the pitfalls below for why.
417+- `sbt-coursier-<sbtVersion>-<scalaBootVersion>`: `bootCoursierCache` ∪ `scalaInstance` ∪ `compilerBridge` in standard Coursier cache layout.
418+
419+The project's own dependencies and plugins are layered on top of `COURSIER_CACHE` at build time instead of being merged in here, precisely to keep the toolchain shareable.
420+
421+`scalaInstance` and `compilerBridge` are unioned over every distinct `scalaVersion` across the build's modules *and* sbt's own `scalaBootVersion` — so a build whose modules disagree on `scalaVersion`, or disagree with sbt's own Scala (always the case on sbt 2, which runs on Scala 3), still resolves offline.
422+
423+#### Build phase (`buildSbtApp`)
424+
425+1. **Source filter** (`prepareSbtSources`): every root-level `*.sbt`, the whole `project/` tree, the locked sources, and the resource directories. `target/` dirs are dropped — they're the sandbox's to create, and a stale local one would both poison the derivation hash and let sbt mistake prebuilt classes for fresh ones.
426+2. **Setup** (`mkSbtEnvSetup`): `cp -rs` the toolchain's boot dir and Coursier cache into writable tmpdirs (sbt writes into both — compiled compiler bridge, internal lockfiles — so the FOD paths can't be used in place; `-rs` symlinks back into the store, so this costs directory entries, not artifact copies), then layer the dependency and plugin caches on top. `HOME` is redirected because the sandbox's is `/homeless-shelter` or `/var/empty`.
427+3. **Build**: `java <opts> -jar <locked sbt-launch.jar> <id>/package ... < /dev/null`, one `<id>/package` per module in the build closure.
428+4. **Install**: each closure module's `packageBin` is copied to `$out/share/<pname>/<id>.jar`, and `makeWrapper` writes `$out/bin/<pname>` running `java -cp <main-scope jars>:<module jars> <mainClass>`.
429+

464+#### Known limitations
465+
466+- Unmanaged (`lib/`) jars aren't locked.
467+- Source generators that invoke external tools, or fetch at generation time, won't work in the sandbox. Self-contained ones (like `BuildInfoPlugin`) do.
468+- `scn init` doesn't scaffold sbt projects yet — write `derivation.nix` by hand (see `examples/sbt-multi/derivation.nix`).
469+- The toolchain derivations aren't reachable as flake outputs, so a public substituter only has them if some build that used them pushed them. Exposing them as packages would let CI cache them once across projects.

111+## sbt projects
112+
113+Projects built by sbt rather than scala-cli use `lock-sbt` and `buildSbtApp`. The approach differs from the other paths: instead of driving the compiler ourselves, **real sbt runs inside the Nix sandbox**, on the version your `project/build.properties` names, against a locked offline installation of sbt itself.
114+
115+```bash
116+cd my-sbt-project
117+scn lock-sbt
118+```
119+
120+This asks sbt what the build looks like — modules, Scala versions, main classes, sources, dependencies, plugins — and writes a `scala.lock.json` with `kind = "sbt"`. Note that it compiles the project once, since sbt's `Compile / mainClass` is a task rather than a setting.
121+
122+Both sbt 1 and sbt 2 are supported (verified against 1.10.7 and 2.1.0).
123+
124+On the Nix side:
125+
126+```nix
127+{ scala-cli-nix }:
128+
129+scala-cli-nix.buildSbtApp {
130+ pname = "my-app";
131+ version = "0.1.0";
132+ src = ./.;
133+ lockFile = ./scala.lock.json;
134+}
135+```
136+
137+### Multi-module builds
138+
139+Each sbt subproject is locked separately. Pass `module` to pick which one to build:
140+
141+```nix
142+scala-cli-nix.buildSbtApp {
143+ pname = "my-app";
144+ version = "0.1.0";
145+ src = ./.;
146+ module = "app"; # an sbt project id
147+ lockFile = ./scala.lock.json;
148+}
149+```
150+
151+The build packages `app` *and* every module it `dependsOn`, transitively, and puts all of their jars on the runtime classpath. `module` may be omitted only when the lockfile has exactly one module — and note that sbt synthesizes an aggregate root project for builds whose `build.sbt` doesn't define one, so a two-module build usually locks as three.
152+
153+`buildSbtApps` builds every module that has a main class, returning an attrset keyed by project id:
154+
155+```nix
156+# Returns: { app = <derivation>; cli = <derivation>; }
157+scala-cli-nix.buildSbtApps { pname = "my-app"; version = "0.1.0"; src = ./.; lockFile = ./scala.lock.json; }
158+```
159+
160+### Tests
161+
162+A module's test scope is exposed as `passthru.tests.test` and runs `<module>/test` offline in the sandbox, so `collectChecks` picks it up alongside the scala-cli examples:
163+
164+```nix
165+checks.${system} = scala-cli-nix.collectChecks self.packages.${system};
166+```
167+
168+### Plugins
169+
170+`project/plugins.sbt` is locked too: plugin coordinates are read from the meta-build and resolved transitively, so plugins work in the sandbox. Source-generating plugins run there as well — `examples/sbt-multi` uses `sbt-buildinfo`, whose generated sources are compiled inside the sandbox like any other.
171+
172+### Caching
173+
174+The sbt installation is split out into two derivations keyed only on `(sbtVersion, scalaBootVersion)` and the locked sbt-side artifact hashes. Nothing project-specific goes into them, so two projects on the same sbt and Scala versions share the exact same store paths, and editing your own source code never rebuilds them.
175+
176+### Limitations
177+
178+- Unmanaged (`lib/`) jars aren't locked.
179+- Source generators that call external tools or fetch at generation time won't work in the sandbox; self-contained ones do.
180+- `scn init` doesn't scaffold sbt projects yet — write `derivation.nix` by hand.
181+

POM dependency version inheritanceRead through

Walks a POM's parent chain to fill in dependency versions that are only declared via an inherited dependencyManagement block, so offline resolution doesn't fail on indirect dependencies. It's shared between the plain scala-cli lock path and the new sbt lock path (the separate coursier-app path does its own JAR-only hashing instead, so this isn't used everywhere). The string-parsing helpers (parseDeclaredDeps, parseDependencyManagement, etc.) are unit tested, but the actual parent-chain walking and merging (collectAccumulatedDependencyManagement, collectDeclaredPoms) — the part most likely to have a bug — has no direct test, so don't just skim this on the assumption it's well covered.

Relevant files

  • cli
    • scala-cli-nix.scala
    • scala-cli-nix.test.scalatest
  • CONTRIBUTING.md

Maven POMs often declare a dependency without a <version> — the version comes from a <dependencyManagement> block somewhere up the POM's <parent> chain. Before this change the lock step just dropped those deps, so their POMs never landed in the lockfile and offline resolution inside the Nix sandbox later failed on them (the real case: jackson-annotations:2.12.1.pom, pulled by sbt's lm-coursier on Linux).

The fix has three parts, all in cli/scala-cli-nix.scala:

  1. parseDeclaredDeps stops dropping version-less deps and reports them with "" as the version.
  2. Two new functions find the inherited version: parseDependencyManagement (one POM) and collectAccumulatedDependencyManagement (that POM plus its whole parent chain, merged).
  3. collectDeclaredPoms — which walks every resolved POM looking for extra artifacts to hash — now fills in the blanks from that map before fetching.

collectDeclaredPoms is called from one place (cli/scala-cli-nix.scala:1048), on the shared path used by both lock and the new lock-sbt. The lock-coords path hashes JARs only and never gets here.

flowchart TD
  P[resolved POM on disk] -->|content| D["parseDeclaredDeps"]
  P -->|parent chain| M["collectAccumulatedDependencyManagement"]
  D -->|"(g, a, v) — v may be empty"| F{"v empty?"}
  M -->|"(g,a) → v map"| F
  F -->|"yes: look up (g,a)"| C[candidate deps]
  F -->|no: keep v| C
  C -->|fetch + sha256| E[ArtifactEntry list in lockfile]

Filling in inherited versions

parseDeclaredDeps(pomContent: String): List[(String, String, String)] is unchanged in shape — it still returns one triple per <dependency> in <dependencies>. The only difference is that a missing <version> now yields "" instead of skipping the whole entry.

parseDependencyManagement(pomContent, properties): Map[(String, String), String] is pure. It reads one POM's <dependencyManagement> section and returns a (group, artifact) → version map. It skips entries with <scope>import</scope> (those are BOM imports, already handled by parseImportedBoms), and it drops any version whose ${...} placeholders don't resolve against properties.

collectAccumulatedDependencyManagement(pomPath, repoBase): IO[Map[(String, String), String]] walks up the <parent> chain and merges all those maps, with the child winning over the ancestor. It follows the same recursion shape as the existing collectAccumulatedProperties (cli/scala-cli-nix.scala:676): resolve the parent's coordinates to a cache path under repoBase, and stop if that file isn't on disk (or if repoBase is empty, which means the POM's URL didn't match the Maven layout). Recursing first and then applying own on top is what gives the child-overrides-ancestor ordering.

Two things worth checking here, since this walk has no direct test:

  • parseDependencyManagement is called with parseProperties(content) — only the current POM's own <properties>. So a managed version written as ${jackson.version} with the property defined in a grandparent will not resolve and gets dropped. The sibling walk for properties (collectAccumulatedProperties) exists and would resolve it; whether that matters in practice depends on how common that layout is.
  • Each level reads the POM file twice (once in loop, once inside extractParent), and readFile doesn't cache. Combined with the existing property and BOM walks, a deep parent chain gets re-read several times. Only lock-time cost, not correctness.

826+/** `(groupId, artifactId) -> version` entries from a POM's own
827+ * `<dependencyManagement>`, excluding `<scope>import</scope>` BOMs (those are
828+ * handled by `parseImportedBoms` / `collectImportedBoms`).
829+ */
830+def parseDependencyManagement(
831+ pomContent: String,
832+ properties: Map[String, String] = Map.empty
833+): Map[(String, String), String] = {
834+ val root = loadPom(pomContent)
835+ val entries = root \ "dependencyManagement" \ "dependencies" \ "dependency"
836+ entries.toList.flatMap { dep =>
837+ val isImport = childText(dep, "scope").contains("import")
838+ if (isImport) Nil
839+ else
840+ parseGAV(dep).toList.flatMap { (g, a, v) =>
841+ val resolved = substituteProperties(v, properties)
842+ Option.when(!resolved.contains("$"))(((g, a), resolved))
843+ }
844+ }.toMap
845+}
846+
847+/** Walk a POM's `<parent>` chain and merge every `<dependencyManagement>`
848+ * section into one `(groupId, artifactId) -> version` map, descendants
849+ * overriding ancestors.
850+ *
851+ * This exists because many POMs declare `<dependency>` blocks with no
852+ * `<version>` — the version is inherited from an ancestor's
853+ * `<dependencyManagement>`. Without this walk those deps are silently dropped
854+ * from the lockfile and offline resolution later fails on them (the concrete
855+ * case that forced it: `jackson-annotations:2.12.1.pom`, needed by sbt's
856+ * lm-coursier on Linux).
857+ *
858+ * Imported BOMs are deliberately *not* expanded here; `collectImportedBoms`
859+ * already walks those.
860+ */
861+def collectAccumulatedDependencyManagement(
862+ pomPath: Path,
863+ repoBase: String
864+): IO[Map[(String, String), String]] = {
865+ def loop(
866+ current: Path,
867+ acc: Map[(String, String), String]
868+ ): IO[Map[(String, String), String]] =
869+ readFile(current).flatMap { content =>
870+ val props = parseProperties(content)
871+ val own = parseDependencyManagement(content, props)
872+ extractParent(current).flatMap {
873+ case Some((g, a, v)) if repoBase.nonEmpty =>
874+ val groupPath = g.replace('.', '/')
875+ val parentUrl = s"$repoBase$groupPath/$a/$v/$a-$v.pom"
876+ val parentPath = cachePathForUrl(parentUrl)
877+ Files[IO].exists(parentPath).flatMap {
878+ case true => loop(parentPath, acc).map(_ ++ own)
879+ case false => IO.pure(acc ++ own)
880+ }
881+ case _ => IO.pure(acc ++ own)
882+ }
883+ }
884+ loop(pomPath, Map.empty)
885+}
886+

Using the map in `collectDeclaredPoms`

Signature and promise are unchanged: given the resolved POM paths and the set of already-resolved URLs, return the extra ArtifactEntry values to add to the lockfile. What changed is the first stage. Per POM it now:

  1. reads the content and derives repoBase from the POM's cache path;
  2. builds the accumulated dependencyManagement map;
  3. parses declared deps and, for each with an empty version, looks up (g, a) in that map — a dep with no entry is dropped, as before.

The rest (filter out unresolved ${...}, skip deps already present in resolvedUrls, fetch each remaining one on its own and tolerate failures) is the old code, just re-indented inside the new .flatMap.
